# Rask

> Rask is the .NET One Person Framework: one developer builds, runs, and ships a whole product — UI,
> data, auth, background work, deployment — from a single C# codebase on one server, with SQLite as the
> production database (no PaaS, no assembled service stack, no second language). The UI is plain C#
> components (a Roslyn generator, scoped CSS/TypeScript, routing) whose same code runs server-rendered
> over WebSockets or client-side on WebAssembly; markup is a chain —
> you name the component and set properties on it (`Div.Class("panel")[Span["hi"]]`), with anything a
> component requires asked for first, so an incomplete component is a compile error rather than a null.
> Batteries: the `rask` CLI, a CQRS+EF CRUD slice pattern, Rask.Cqrs, Rask.Data, production SQLite
> (pragmas + backup),
> auth, background jobs, transactional email, cache, outbox, a durable log store and an operator
> dashboard — and `rask deploy`, which builds and runs the app on one box over SSH with zero-downtime
> blue-green releases, a health-gated cutover, auto-HTTPS via Caddy, and bare-VPS provisioning.

This file helps AI coding assistants build apps with Rask. Start with the repo-root AGENTS.md
(the AI guidance shipped alongside this file) for app-authoring conventions, then the docs below.

## Docs
- [The .NET One Person Framework](docs/one-person-framework.md): the doctrine — one dev, whole product, one C# codebase on one server, SQLite-first; links the batteries + roadmap.
- [Installing Rask](docs/installation.md): the one-line installer, `curl -sSL https://rask.sh/rask.sh | sh` (Windows: `irm https://rask.sh/rask.ps1 | iex`). `rask.sh` and `rask.ps1` live at the repo ROOT and are published to GitHub Pages by `pages.yml`. They install the .NET 10 SDK into `~/.dotnet` (via Microsoft's dotnet-install.sh, run with BASH — it is a bash script, and `sh` silently works on macOS then dies on Debian), `Rask.Cli`, `dotnet-ef`, the `wasm-tools` workload and Node LTS (SHA-256 verified against nodejs.org's SHASUMS256.txt) into `~/.local/share/rask/node`, then run `rask doctor`. Everything under `$HOME` — no sudo, no distro package manager; an SDK already present is DETECTED AND LEFT ALONE (any major ≥ 10, because `RollForward=Major`). Docker is detected and reported, NEVER installed — only `rask deploy` needs it. Re-running upgrades and rewrites its `PATH` block rather than appending. Flags: `--version <v>`, `--prerelease`, `--no-sdk|-ef|-wasm-tools|-node|-path`, `--dry-run`, `--quiet`, `--help`; through a pipe use `sh -s -- --flag`; an unknown flag exits 2. TRUNCATION SAFETY is structural, not a warning: every statement is inside a function and the file's last line is the only call, so a dropped `curl | sh` runs nothing — `scripts/tests/install-script.test.sh` proves it by executing prefixes of the real file, and also pins the install URL byte-identically across all nine files that carry it. `scripts/run-install-e2e-local.sh` runs the script in containers with no .NET/Node at all (pre-push, path-gated on `rask.sh`/`rask.ps1`). A missing ICU is diagnosed by name — dotnet-install.sh unpacks a tarball and installs no native dependencies, so on a slim image the SDK installs and then cannot run.
- [Getting started](docs/getting-started.md): install, first app, project layout; the root component (`TApp`) renders into `<body>` and Rask composes the document around it — doctype, `<html lang>` from the `HtmlLang` override, a `<head>` collected from every mounted component's `Head` override plus the scoped CSS/JS, and a `<body>` (class from `BodyClass`) holding the render output and the auto-appended runtime `<script>`; `Shell(head, body)` is the escape hatch for a custom document (it takes the framework's `<head>` and the rendered body as parameters, runs once per render BEFORE `Render()`, and dropping `head` loses every head asset). A root that renders `Doctype`/`Html`/`Head`/`Body` itself is RASK021 — the nested document is silently unwrapped by the parser, so there is no runtime check, only the analyzer.
- **[The `Rask` package + `RaskApp`](docs/getting-started.md)**: the ONE reference an application takes. `Rask` is a meta-package over `Rask.Server` PLUS every battery (data, cqrs+query, jobs, mail, cache, outbox, dashboard, logging, webpush, sqlite snapshots+litestream, wasm hosting), and it carries `RaskApp`/`RaskAppOptions`. **`var app = RaskApp.Create(args); app.Run<App>();` is a complete app with EVERY BATTERY ON** — referencing the package is what turns them on, there is nothing to opt into and no `AddRaskX` to write, so a `Program.cs` with no `Configure` block means "all of them" and only the EXCEPTIONS are written: `app.Configure(c => { c.Jobs.Off(); c.Mail.Configure(o => o.From = "…"); })`. Turning one off takes its dependents with it (`c.Data.Off()` drops jobs/mail/cache/outbox/snapshots/ops; `c.Cqrs.Off()` drops data; Logs owns its own file and is never dropped). Battery configuration is RECORDED AND REPLAYED onto the battery's own options instance, which is what lets `c.Mail.Configure(…)` sit beside `c.Jobs.Off()` while every options type stays `sealed`. **Nothing has to be turned off in order to configure it**: the automatic wiring runs LAST (from `Build`, after every `Configure` and after everything `Program.cs` registered) and every `AddRaskX` is idempotent — keeping the FIRST registration's options and, because `AddHostedService` uses `TryAddEnumerable`, exactly one worker — so a direct `app.Services.AddRaskMail<Ctx>(…)` simply wins. **The DbContext names itself**: the DB-backed pillars need a `TContext`, and the app already wrote `AddDbContextFactory<AppDbContext>()`, so the type is read off that registration rather than discovered or declared (this deleted an earlier source generator, its `[ModuleInitializer]` bridge and a RASK057 diagnostic entirely). `RaskApp` also owns the middleware order once instead of in four scaffolder emitters: forwarded headers (opt-in via `c.BehindProxy` — trusting them from an arbitrary client lets it forge its own IP), `/health` BEFORE `UseHttpsRedirection` (else `rask deploy`'s plain-HTTP probe 307s to a dead port), HSTS/exception handler outside Development, static assets (SKIPPED WITH A WARNING when the build produced no manifest, which is every non-Web-SDK host — it otherwise throws), `RunBeforeDatabaseOpensAsync` (a Litestream restore that runs after the first query has already lost), `UseAuthentication`/`UseAuthorization` ONLY when a scheme is registered (it throws otherwise) and always before `UseRask` (RASK024), then `MapEndpoints` — a named seam, because an endpoint mapped after `UseRask`'s catch-all never runs AND never errors, it renders the app where the author expected JSON — then `UseRask<TApp>`. `c.Wasm = true` is the whole browser rung in one switch (render-mode ceiling + `AddRaskWasmHost()` + `UseRaskWasmAssets()`/`UseRouting()` in position). `c.Cultures` names the languages; **`AddRask` is called from `Build`, not `Create`**, because its options register with `TryAddSingleton` so the first call wins — calling it eagerly would freeze the culture list before `Configure` ran and ship an app with no languages while `Program.cs` listed some (that is RASK056). Two batteries THROW without configuration and so get booting defaults: snapshots (`snapshots/`, or `Sqlite:SnapshotDirectory`) and mail (`no-reply@example.com` — IANA-reserved, so an app that never sets it cannot send as a real domain). Consequence of on-by-default: a running app writes `logs.db`, `mail-pickup/` and `snapshots/` beside itself (gitignored by `rask new`). **`Rask.Server` is unchanged and stays lean** — reference it directly for a host with no EF Core and no SQLite natives; that door is why `Rask` is a separate package rather than a change to it.
- [Tutorial: zero to deploy](docs/tutorial/00-overview.md): a step-by-step build of a "Shop" app that adds every OPF pillar in order — scaffold (`rask new`), first DB-backed feature (the chapter writes the entity, EF configuration, CQRS handlers and pages as code, plus the `AddRaskCqrs`/`AddRaskData`/`AddDbContextFactory` DI, then `rask db add/update`), auth (`[Authorize]` + the `Authorize` component), background jobs (`IBackgroundJob` + a handler + `AddRaskJobs<Ctx>` + `IJob`), transactional email (a body component + `AddRaskMail<Ctx>` + `IMail`), cache (`AddRaskCache<Ctx>` + `ICache.GetOrAddAsync`), domain events/outbox (`IOutboxEvent` + `AddRaskOutbox<Ctx>`), production SQLite (`UseRaskSqlite` + `AddRaskSqliteLitestream`), and `rask deploy --host --domain` to one box. 11 chapters under docs/tutorial/, each the code to write + a verify step; ch1 scaffolds with a plain `rask new Shop --auth` (every battery is on by default) so every later chapter teaches what a pillar is FOR rather than how to wire it, ch9 = Web Push, ch10 = an /ops page over every pillar's table (then points at the built-in `Rask.Dashboard` that ships the finished version), ch11 = deploy. The finished app is committed as samples/Rask.Example.Shop (browser-tested), which is where to look when a snippet needs its surroundings.
- [The `rask` CLI](docs/cli.md): the optional `Rask.Cli` .NET tool (`curl -sSL https://rask.sh/rask.sh | sh` installs it together with the .NET 10 SDK, dotnet-ef, the wasm-tools workload and Node, all under $HOME with no sudo — `rask.ps1` is the Windows twin, `dotnet tool install -g Rask.Cli` the SDK-already-present path, and docs/installation.md the reference) — a thin wrapper over the SDK with two package references: SQLite (for `rask db backup`, which needs the Online Backup API to copy a live WAL database without tearing it) and Spectre.Console (the whole terminal surface — help pages, `deploy status`/`doctor` tables, spinners, and the `rask new` wizard). Piped output carries no escape codes and is never reflowed, and spinners write nothing at all off a terminal, so `rask doctor | grep` and CI logs read exactly as before; `NO_COLOR` strips every escape while keeping the cursor control the prompts need. **`rask` with no arguments opens the new-project wizard on a terminal** (piped, it still prints the command list): name, an arrow-key project type, styling, an auth question, and a space-toggled battery checklist that arrives FULLY TICKED (space unticks; pressing enter through it equals a bare `rask new`) — filling gaps rather than re-asking, so anything already on the command line is kept and its question skipped. **BATTERIES ARE INCLUDED**: `rask new <name> [--template server|wasm|react|preact|vue|angular|solid|svelte|lit] [--auth] [--wasm] [--no-pwa] [--no-cqrs] [--no-data] [--no-jobs] [--no-mail] [--no-cache] [--no-outbox] [--no-push] [--no-snapshots] [--no-logs] [--no-ops] [--no-docker] [--no-git] [--no-restore] [--output]` turns on EVERY battery the chosen template supports and generates the project directly (the CLI owns all scaffolding — no `dotnet new`, no separate templates package); server is the default template. The default set is literally `template.SupportedFlags` minus `auth`, so nobody maintains a per-template default list. **`OptInFlags` is gone** (#854): localization was its only member and it stopped being a flag at all — languages are configured in Program.cs, never on the command line, because a flag would only restate at scaffold time what the file goes on being the truth about. A server app starts with "en" registered in its AddRask(configureCulture:) block and adding another is a line there; a browser-WASM app registers none, since a language in the browser means shipping ICU (~1 MB, +32% on the showcase) and <RaskGlobalization> is an MSBuild property Program.cs cannot reach — it is scaffolded COMMENTED OUT with the reason beside it. `--culture` and `--no-localization` are REFUSED by name, not ignored: --culture took a value, so swallowing it would scaffold English while the command line said Hungarian. **`--auth`, `--wasm` and styling are the only three things it asks you** — they change what the app IS rather than what it can do. `--wasm` (server template only) turns on the ONE-PROJECT BUILD: `<RaskBrowserRung>true</RaskBrowserRung>` plus `RenderModes.Wasm`, `AddRaskWasmHost()` and `app.UseRaskWasmAssets()` mapped BEFORE an explicitly-written `app.UseRouting()`, so `dotnet publish` generates a second project into obj/ carrying the WebAssembly SDK, compiles this app's OWN sources into it (minus Program.cs and Server/**, while the SERVER excludes Browser/** — the mirror convention, and the only place a file may use a RaskBrowserPackageReference, since that package is absent from the server by design) and publishes the bundle into wwwroot — one authored project, both halves, and an eligible page moves into WebAssembly on the next navigation once the bundle has downloaded. Publish-only, since linking a WASM runtime takes minutes and buys nothing in development. Every battery has a `--no-<battery>` to leave it out, and turning one off takes its dependents with it (`--no-data` also drops jobs/mail/cache/outbox/snapshots/ops; `--no-cqrs` also drops data; `--no-pwa` also drops push; `--no-logs` drops nothing, since the log store owns its own file). **The positive flags are REMOVED, not kept as no-ops** — `--data`, `--jobs`, `--all-batteries` etc. fail with a message naming the `--no-` replacement, because an accepted-and-disregarded flag is this repo's most expensive bug class. `--no-<battery>` for something the template never had is a usage error naming what it does support; `--no-cqrs` on a front-end template is refused outright (the generated TypeScript wire IS the mediator). **`rask new` also CREATES AND APPLIES THE FIRST MIGRATION** (delegating to `rask db`, so it installs dotnet-ef and adds Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design exactly as `rask db add` would), because the DB-backed pillars are hosted services and one that cannot find its table STOPS THE HOST — without it the first `dotnet run` of every new project would exit rather than warn; `--no-restore` skips it and a failure is a warning plus the two manual commands, never a failed scaffold. The database (implies cqrs) pre-wires a SQLite database — an empty `AppDbContext` + `AddRaskData()` + a `UseRaskSqlite` (WAL/`busy_timeout`) `AddDbContextFactory<AppDbContext>` whose connection string honours a `ConnectionStrings:App` override — so your first entity attaches to it and is immediately runnable with `rask db add`/`update`; the **batteries** (server template; Web Push is server-only) each add their package + `AddRaskX<AppDbContext>()` + the `modelBuilder.AddRaskX()` schema call — jobs/mail/cache/outbox (all need the database, so `--no-data` drops them), Web Push (needs the PWA, so `--no-pwa` drops it; VAPID + `/_push/{key,subscribe,unsubscribe}` + a subscription store), snapshots (scheduled Online-Backup-API copies; continuous Litestream backup rides the database, config-gated on `Litestream:ReplicaUrl`, with `RaskLitestreamDownload=false` so builds stay offline), ops (the `/_rask` operator dashboard — needs the database; emits an `AddAuthorization` policy for `RaskDashboardPolicies.Access` when `--auth` is on and a commented one when it isn't, because without a policy the dashboard denies everyone outside Development; in a client-plus-host solution it also references Rask.Server and mounts `app.UseRaskServer<RaskDashboardShell>("/_rask/{**path}")` ABOVE the SPA's MapFallback, so the dashboard is server-rendered while the client keeps every other route); the composed Program.cs gets the load-bearing order right (`ApplyRaskConventions()` AFTER the entity configurations since it walks the model as it stands — the outbox no longer has to precede the DbContext factory, since that callback runs when the factory is first resolved and so sees every registration whenever it was made) and **`AddRaskData()` is emitted BARE even with the outbox on**: `AddRaskOutbox` claims domain-event delivery itself by registering an `IDomainEventDeliveryOwner` read when the container is built, rather than from a `DispatchDomainEventsInProcess = false` the author had to remember. Forgetting it — or writing the two Add calls in the other order — ran both interceptors, and DomainEventInterceptor drains and clears each entity's events in SavingChanges before OutboxInterceptor can copy them, so the outbox stayed permanently empty and delivery quietly stopped being durable while every in-process handler still ran, failing nothing; **`--wasm` WIRES REMOTE DISPATCH** — AddRaskCqrsServer() + MapRaskCqrs() on the server, Rask.Cqrs.Client as a BROWSER-ONLY reference (`RaskBrowserPackageReference`, so the client transport never reaches the process that answers its endpoints) and a Browser/BrowserStartup.cs whose Configure the bundle calls via `RaskBrowserStartup`; messages are shared by construction (one project, both halves) and handlers stay out of the download by living under Server/. Without `--auth` it sets RequireAuthenticatedUser=false with a comment saying why — there is no authentication to require, and the secure default left on would make every message answer 401; `--output` overrides the target directory; **every** template also writes a `.gitignore`, an `.editorconfig` and a `<Name>.slnx`, and initializes a git repository with one commit AFTER the first migration, so `Migrations/` is in it (`--no-git` opts out; skipped automatically inside an existing repo) — the things whose absence is paid for later by someone else. **Styling is not a decision: Tailwind is built in** — there is no flag, no package to add and no off switch. Every template scaffolds a `Styles/app.css` holding one `@import "tailwindcss"` (no config file, no content array, no PostCSS — v4 detects the sources itself, C# string literals included) and the host package compiles it at build time; on the front-end templates it goes through the client's OWN bundler instead. There is no `Rask.Bootstrap` any more. `rask db <add|remove|list|update|drop|backup|restore> [<name|file>] [--project/-p] [--startup-project/-s] [--context/-c] [--output/-o] [--remote] [--host] [--app] [--yes/-y] [-- ef args]` wraps `dotnet ef` for the migration lifecycle (add/remove/list migrations, update/drop the database), resolving the project from the single .csproj at/above the CWD and installing `dotnet-ef` globally on first use if missing; `backup`/`restore` never touch EF — a file copy of a live SQLite database is NOT a backup (with WAL on, committed transactions sit in the -wal sidecar until a checkpoint, so the .db alone is torn or stale), so both go through SQLite: locally via Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's Online Backup API, remotely via `VACUUM INTO` inside a throwaway `alpine` container mounted on the app's `<slug>-data` volume, fetched with `docker cp` over the existing `docker -H ssh://` connection (nothing installed on the host; host/app default from `.rask/deploy.json`, `--host`/`--app` override, and the host string goes through the same SshTarget parser so a leading-`-` value can never reach ssh as an option). `restore` behaves like `drop` — prompts unless `--yes`, refuses when there is no terminal — and `--remote` STOPS the app first and starts it after, deleting the `-wal`/`-shm` sidecars with the old file, because replacing a database under a live writer (or leaving a stale WAL beside it) yields a corrupted hybrid; `rask dev [--project] [--urls] [--launch-profile] [--open|--no-open] [--no-hot-reload] [--no-restart] [--once] [--no-banner] [-- app args]` runs `dotnet watch run`, resolving the project itself (the `.Server` host in a client-plus-host solution), setting `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development` when unset and the `HotReloadAutoRestart` MSBuild property so an edit hot reload cannot apply restarts instead of stalling on watch's interactive prompt (`--no-restart` to be asked); `--no-hot-reload` keeps watching and restarts on change (`--once` is a plain `dotnet run`). Component `Render()` bodies, scoped `.css`/`.js`, `[Route]` templates, CQRS handlers and job/outbox registrations all hot-reload; adding a type or changing a signature is a rude edit that restarts. In Development the browser shows a brief "Hot reload applied" pill and a restart reloads the page in ~250ms, and a build that FAILS is reported as a build failure rather than as a lost connection — `rask dev` reads watch's output and serves the compiler errors from a loopback status endpoint it owns (stamped onto every page as `data-rask-dev-status`, so the browser can still ask after the app process is gone), which the client polls on a drop and paints in a corner panel instead of "Reconnecting…" over a "Retry now" that cannot work; the reconnect backoff keeps running underneath, so fixing the code brings the app back on its own; `rask deploy [--host user@box] [--domain app.example.com] [--port] [--name] [--project] [--dockerfile] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--env-file] [--health-path] [--no-health-check] [--github-actions] [--dry-run] [--setup-host|--no-setup-host] [--deploy-user <name>|--no-deploy-user] [--no-firewall] [--no-harden-ssh]` builds+runs the app on a single host over SSH (every *deploy* op is `docker -H ssh://host …` — no registry/local daemon; builds on the box), remembering host/domain in `.rask/deploy.json` (never secrets); `--domain` fronts it with a shared auto-HTTPS Caddy proxy (Let's Encrypt) and deploys are zero-downtime blue-green, gated on an HTTP health check (`GET /health` — scaffolded by `rask new`; `--health-path` overrides, `--no-health-check` skips) so a container that starts but fails its probe never takes traffic, with multiple apps sharing one box (routing regenerated from each container's `rask.*` labels), no `--domain` publishes `--port` (default 8080) for your own proxy. Every deploy mounts a per-app named Docker volume for the SQLite database (`-v <slug>-data:/data` + `ConnectionStrings__App=Data Source=/data/app.db`) so the DB survives container replacement across redeploys, and stops the retiring container gracefully (SIGTERM, `docker stop -t 20`) before removing it so its Litestream replicator flushes and SQLite checkpoints the WAL (a plain `rm -f`/SIGKILL would drop the last frames); the `rask new` Dockerfile prepares a writable `/data` owned by the non-root runtime user (`mkdir -p /data && chown $APP_UID`), which a custom Dockerfile must replicate. **Handed a bare VPS it sets the box up first** (the one non-docker remote path — installing Docker over `docker -H ssh://` is chicken-and-egg, so setup shells out to plain `ssh`): one read-only probe reports what the box has, then after showing the list and asking once (`--setup-host` skips the prompt, required when there's no terminal; `--no-setup-host` refuses to touch the host) it installs Docker from get.docker.com, creates a non-root `deploy` login with your `authorized_keys` + docker group + NOPASSWD sudo (`--deploy-user`/`--no-deploy-user`) and rewrites the remembered host to it, enables ufw (sshd's real ports read off the box + 80/443 or `--port`, default-deny inbound; `--no-firewall`) and puts Docker's published ports behind it — Docker's own iptables rules are reached through FORWARD and never meet ufw's INPUT rules, so a stock box serves every `-p` port to the internet while `ufw status` calls it denied; Rask writes a fenced block into `/etc/ufw/after.rules` (so it survives a reboot) that default-denies anything forwarded into a Docker bridge except the container port this deploy publishes, with `ufw route allow` as the way to open more, and hardens sshd via `/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-rask.conf` (`--no-harden-ssh`). Idempotent — a ready box is left alone with no prompt. Safety: nothing that can revoke access runs until a *fresh* connection (`ControlPath=none`) proves the new login drives docker; root login is only disabled once a non-root one exists; firewall+hardening run behind a `systemd-run` rollback timer on the host that reverts both after ~5min unless disarmed, so a lockout heals even if the CLI dies; and anything unprovable is skipped loudly (no sshd port readable → no firewall). `--github-actions` writes `.github/workflows/deploy.yml` (push to main → same `rask deploy`, `--no-setup-host` so CI never provisions) + prints the two `gh secret set` lines (`RASK_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY`, `RASK_SSH_KNOWN_HOSTS`); host/domain come from the committed `.rask/deploy.json`. `rask info` reports CLI/SDK/OS (`--json` for scripts); `rask doctor` runs every environment probe the other commands own — SDK, dotnet-ef, Docker, project/template/provider detection, and the `.rask/*.json` configs — read-only, warnings not failures, `--json` for CI; `rask --version`. Tailwind reaches EVERY template including browser-WASM (it ships inside the host packages, build-only — no runtime assembly — and on wasm the stylesheet belongs to the browser project, because Tailwind v4 detects sources relative to where it runs); on the front-end templates it goes through the client's OWN bundler instead (`@tailwindcss/vite` in the Vite config Rask writes, or `@tailwindcss/postcss` via a `.postcssrc.json` for Angular, whose Vite config belongs to `@angular/build` — install the wrong one and every utility is missing from the output with nothing reporting it) and REPLACES the scaffolder's global stylesheet, which has to carry a `@layer base` styling the elements the starter renders: part of the file being replaced styles the placeholder page the overlay removed, but the rest styles `body`/`h1`/`p` BY TAG and those tags are what the starter still renders, so a bare `@import "tailwindcss"` plus Tailwind's preflight left the page as unstyled HTML — visibly worse than no flag — while every check stayed green, because the build gate injected its own probe class and so only ever proved the compiler runs; the starters' markup is byte-identical with and without the flag and carries no `class` attributes, which is why the utilities are applied by element; the front-end templates also scaffold the PWA and Web Push, with the manifest/icon/service-worker in the CLIENT's `public/` (every bundler copies it to the bundle root, so it works under the dev server too, where a host-served worker would 404 — and a service worker that 404s once is never retried), NO app-shell cache (the bundler fingerprints assets and rewrites index.html each build, so a cached shell points at files that no longer exist — installable and push-capable but NOT offline), and both URLs patched into index.html ROOT-ABSOLUTE because a SPA serves one document at every route (a relative manifest 404s on a deep link and register("rask-sw.js") would scope the worker to that sub-tree and never see a push); `src/rask/push.ts` is vendored against `GET /_push/key` + `POST /_push/{subscribe,unsubscribe}` and its one load-bearing line flattens the browser's nested `{endpoint, keys:{p256dh,auth}}` into the flat `PushSubscription(Endpoint,P256dh,Auth)` the host binds — post the nested shape and the request STILL answers 204 with both keys null, and every later send fails to encrypt. Rask.Query rides along with the dispatcher rather than having a flag of its own (reference AND `AddRaskQuery()`), and stays its own package depending on BOTH Rask.Cqrs and Rask.Core because it is the composition of them — Rask.Cqrs.Server and Rask.Spa.Hosting reference no Rask.Core at all, so a TypeScript-SPA host runs the mediator with zero component runtime.
- [Live playground](docs/playground.md): write Rask component C# in the browser with a real IDE and see it compile + render live — Roslyn + the Rask source generator run entirely in WebAssembly (no server), the emitted component is Assembly.Load-ed and mounted as a child of the playground's own tree so its handlers/state run through the shared live session. The editor has Roslyn `CompletionService` IntelliSense and as-you-type diagnostics (CS + RASK) as inline Monaco squiggles, driven by a workspace-backed analysis path that never Emits/loads (so typing can't leak assemblies — only Run does); a left-hand pane offers two tabs — a Counter / Form+validation / Todo example gallery, and an eight-chapter guided **tutorial** (Ctrl/Cmd+Enter runs). Tutorial chapters 1–4 cover components/state/composition/forms; chapters 5–8 run **real EF Core + SQLite in the browser tab** (`e_sqlite3` linked into the WASM runtime via a native relink), teaching `Rask.Data`'s `Entity<Guid>` + `ApplyRaskConventions()` + auditing/soft-delete interceptors — the same conventions the tutorial uses. Each chapter owns its own database file in the runtime's in-memory filesystem (lost on reload, by design); a build made with `-p:WasmBuildNative=false` ships without the EF Core reference set and marks those chapters read-only. The `samples/Rask.Example.Playground` app, published to GitHub Pages at `/rask/playground/` next to the showcase; ships untrimmed (Roslyn reads the `_framework/*.dll` back as metadata references, so WasmEnableWebcil=false; Microsoft.CodeAnalysis.CSharp.Features adds CompletionService), user code always runs interpreted, entry point is a `Playground : Component` in a namespace.
- [Best practices](docs/best-practices.md): production patterns + common pitfalls across components, state, forms, data, security, accessibility, performance, testing (each links the deep dive).
- [Building components](docs/building-components.md): how markup is written — naming a component and chaining onto it; the properties a component demands BEFORE it exists (required ones are steps, in any order, and the component appears only once none are outstanding); bound (`Input.Bind(() => m.Name)`) versus controlled (`Input.Value(v)`) form controls, which are mutually exclusive by construction — the opening step fixes the mode in the chain's type (`Build<T, Bound>` / `Build<T, Controlled>`), so the other mode's steps are not offered at all: no `Value`/`Checked`/`OnInput`/`OnChange` on a bound chain, no `Validate`/`AfterBind` on a controlled one, while everything belonging to neither stays reachable from both; type arguments always inferred from the opening step; and callback properties declared as ordinary delegates (`Action?`, `Func<T, Task>?`) whose chain step shares the property's name.
- [Elements & the DSL](docs/elements.md): the render surface — the primitives (`Text` HTML-encodes, `Raw` is verbatim, `Doctype` — for documents you build by hand, since an app's own shell is the framework's) and the `[...]` collection expression for sibling fragments; a generator-emitted chain entry for every HTML and SVG element; the universal props on every tag (`Id`/`Class`/`Style`/`Title`/`Data`/`Role`/`TabIndex`/`Aria`, the rest of HTML's global attributes — `Lang`/`Dir`/`Hidden`/`Inert`/`Popover`/`ContentEditable`/`Spellcheck`/`Translate`/`Draggable` — and `Attributes`, the verbatim escape hatch for anything unnamed, in a fixed attribute render order); typed SVG components (no `Raw()`); and the full HTML-element catalog by category.
- [Routing](docs/routing.md): `[Route]`, params, `Router()`/`Outlet()`, navigation.
- [Lifecycle](docs/lifecycle.md): OnMount/OnPropsChanged/OnRendered/OnUnmount, async hooks.
- [Render modes](docs/render-modes.md): the initial GET waits for async data; a page needing nothing live is served as a cacheable document with no session; `IPageResponse.SetStatus`; redirect on load via `Navigator`.
- [Composition](docs/composition.md): the three component tiers (static method vs stateless vs stateful component), children, context (provide/consume), callbacks, toast messages (`IToaster` — scoped-per-session, consumed-once transient messages that survive a client-side navigation; drained by a headless `ToastOutlet`, which a toast outlet of your own renders), the full DOM `GlobalEventHandlers` event surface on every element (mouse/pointer/touch/wheel/focus/keyboard/clipboard/drag as typed `OnX`+`OnXAsync` pairs; Audio/Video add the `HTMLMediaElement` events), headless primitives (`Virtualize.Items<T>`, the one method-call entry point on the surface because its `T` comes from the render delegate rather than an opening chain step), drag-and-drop, and `Mount(Child: instance)` for hosting a component the app built itself (a runtime-chosen type, a plugin, code compiled in the browser) — such an instance never passes through a chain step.s `GetOrCreate`, so without `Mount` it renders but gets NO lifecycle at all (no `OnMount`/`OnMountAsync`/`OnRendered`/`OnUnmount`) and no handle to re-render through, leaving anything that loads in `OnMountAsync` stuck on its placeholder.
- [Forms](docs/forms.md): binding, validation, EditContext, building form components — implement `IFormControl<T>` (Rask.Core.Forms) on a generic component and the generator synthesizes its controlled + bound chains, or use the public binding API directly (`ExpressionAccessor`/`BindingHelpers`/`RegisterFieldValidator`). `IFormControl<T>` is the framework primitive; ready-made typed radio-group/checkbox-group/multi-select controls are yours to build (docs/building-form-controls.md walks one). The a bound form control auto-wires `aria-invalid` + `aria-describedby` + a `role="alert"` error region when its field is invalid.
- [Building form controls](docs/building-form-controls.md): end-to-end guide to authoring a custom control with `IFormControl<T>` — the interface, a complete worked example, the default-method helpers, and the bound-vs-controlled / stateless-helper-vs-Component trade-offs.
- [HTTP & files](docs/http-and-files.md): data & file *transfer* — a DI'd `HttpClient` (constructor-injected, `BaseAddress` at the app origin; fetch in `OnMountAsync` with cancel/retry/error handling), the typed file-picker input (`Input<string>().Type(InputType.File).Files(…)` + `RaskFile` metadata; multipart on Server, JS chunked reads on WASM), and `Navigator.Download` (event-handler-only; served from `/_rask/download/…` on Server, base64 to JS on WASM).
- [Data access](docs/data-access.md): EF Core + SQLite, IDbContextFactory, loading in the lifecycle, vertical slices, DDD value objects, decimal on SQLite (invariant collation).
- [SQLite production pragmas](docs/sqlite.md): the opt-in `Rask.SQLite` package — applies a production SQLite pragma set (journal_mode=WAL, synchronous=NORMAL, foreign_keys=ON, busy_timeout=5000, cache_size=2000 pages, mmap_size=128MiB, journal_size_limit=64MiB; temp_store opt-in) to every connection. Raw ADO.NET: `services.AddRaskSqlite(cs, configure?)` + inject `ISqlite`. Per-connection pragmas are re-applied on every pooled open (only journal_mode=WAL persists in the file); each option is overridable or nullable-to-skip via `SqlitePragmaOptions`. CONCURRENT WRITES: `factory.InImmediateTransactionAsync(async (conn, ct) => …)` runs the work in a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` transaction and acquires the write lock through the raw sqlite3 handle with the native busy handler off — the only wait is an `await Task.Delay` at a CONSTANT 1ms fair interval (not exponential backoff) that FREES the thread rather than blocking it inside native code; `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` takes the write lock up front, converting the otherwise UNRETRYABLE deferred read-then-write dead-lock into a plain waitable wait. The work delegate runs AT LEAST ONCE, not exactly once: SQLite may roll a transaction back itself when a contended COMMIT is answered with SQLITE_BUSY (sqlite3_get_autocommit is the only way to detect it), so the whole transaction is re-run from BEGIN — retrying the COMMIT alone would only meet the non-retryable "cannot commit - no transaction is active". Re-running is bounded by the same Timeout measured from entry, then surfaces SQLITE_ABORT_ROLLBACK. Keep the delegate re-runnable, put non-repeatable side effects outside it, and never issue COMMIT/ROLLBACK/END inside it (a transaction that ends during the delegate is reported, not retried, because kept-vs-discarded cannot be told apart). Also `connection.BeginImmediate()` (returns a SqliteTransaction; spells out at the call site what BeginTransaction() already does by default, so it cannot quietly become deferred; its wait blocks the thread inside Microsoft.Data.Sqlite) and `connection.InImmediateTransactionAsync(retry, work)`. `SqliteBusyRetryOptions` (Timeout=5s, PollInterval=1ms) via `AddRaskSqlite(cs, configure?, configureRetry?)`. Base package depends ONLY on Microsoft.Data.Sqlite and is reflection-free → works server-side and under trimming/AOT. NOT for the browser/WASM — but only because its PRAGMAS don't apply there (one connection, no concurrency to tame), not because SQLite can't run: it does. Browser companion `Rask.SQLite.Browser` (docs/sqlite.md#rasksqlitebrowser--keeping-a-browser-database): `services.AddRaskBrowserSqlite("app")` + `o.UseSqlite(BrowserSqlite.ConnectionString("app"))` gives a WASM app a real, reload-surviving SQLite database — restored from IndexedDB inside a hosted service's StartAsync (so anything registered after it opens a populated file), written back on SnapshotInterval (default 30s) and on pagehide via the Online Backup API, single-owner across tabs via a Web Lock. The native e_sqlite3 needs NO wiring: the pinned SQLitePCLRaw 3.x bundle resolves to a native package that ships runtimes/browser-wasm/e_sqlite3.a and adds the NativeFileReference itself when RuntimeIdentifier=browser-wasm. HARD CONSTRAINTS: publish WITHOUT -p:WasmBuildNative=false (no relink => no SQLite => boots fine then fails every DB call), and PublishTrimmed=false (EF Core dies in the trimmer: MissingMethodException on EntryCurrentValueComparer<int>; raw Microsoft.Data.Sqlite survives it), plus NoWarn=WASM0001 for the varargs sqlite3_config natives. Durability window = the snapshot interval, NOT the pagehide flush (the browser does not wait for it). Non-owner tabs get their own EMPTY, unpersisted database — not a view of the owner's; promotion and write-proxying are not implemented. Use journal_mode=DELETE not WAL (one connection, and DELETE leaves the file consistent at rest, which is what makes its bytes shippable). Working app: samples/Rask.Example.Wasm.Jobs (Rask.Jobs running in the browser). For a JS-native client DB, the sqlite-wasm+OPFS stack in a Web Worker is still the only way to read/write OPFS pages directly. EF Core integration is a SEPARATE package `Rask.SQLite.EntityFrameworkCore`: `o.UseRaskSqlite(cs, configure?, configureRetry?)` (drop-in for UseSqlite; ConnectionOpened interceptor; pulls in Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Sqlite) — split out so the base stays EF-free for mobile/AOT. Passing configureRetry (even empty) registers a fair-interval `RaskSqliteExecutionStrategy` so SaveChanges/queries retry on SQLITE_BUSY/SQLITE_LOCKED (turns busy_timeout=0 and lowers Microsoft.Data.Sqlite's command timeout so the async strategy owns the wait; each EF command still routes through the driver's synchronous busy-retry so a contended attempt can block ~1s before the strategy takes over — the raw InImmediateTransactionAsync path has no such floor; EVERY transaction EF opens on SQLite is ALREADY BEGIN IMMEDIATE — the implicit SaveChanges one and Database.BeginTransaction[Async]() alike — because Microsoft.Data.Sqlite emits BEGIN IMMEDIATE for ADO.NET's default Serializable isolation and EF's Unspecified normalises to it; nothing needs wrapping, and the only deferred trapdoor is asking for it (IsolationLevel.ReadUncommitted, or the deferred:true overload). Pinned by RaskSqliteTransactionModeTests. The real EF read-then-write hazard is a LOST UPDATE — the read usually happens OUTSIDE any transaction, so the fix is a concurrency token, not a transaction mode). Backup companion `Rask.SQLite.Litestream` (docs/sqlite.md#continuous-backup-with-litestream): managed Litestream supervisor — `services.AddRaskSqliteLitestream(o => { o.DatabasePath; o.ReplicaUrl="s3://…"|"gcs://…"|"abs://…"|"file://…"; o.ConfigPath?; o.RestoreOnStartup=true; o.ShutdownGracePeriod=10s; })` registers a hosted BackgroundService that runs `litestream replicate` for the process lifetime (graceful SIGINT flush on shutdown), plus `await app.Services.RestoreSqliteFromLitestreamAsync()` to restore from the replica before opening the DB (no-op if the file exists). Runs the litestream binary via CliWrap (set ExecutablePath if not on PATH). Single-writer only; DB on local disk not a network share; ideal for ephemeral containers / Azure App Service Linux (DB on local disk, replicate to abs://, single instance, Always On). Backup failures log Critical, never crash the app. Resolve the `LitestreamStatus` singleton to read replication liveness in code (`Current.IsReplicating`/`LastStartedAt`/`LastExitedAt`/`RestartCount`/`LastExitCode`/`LastError`) — a clean shutdown clears IsReplicating without counting a restart, so a climbing RestartCount means backups are flapping. RESTORABILITY IS A DIFFERENT FACT from liveness, and every field above describes only the local child process: a replica writing to the wrong prefix, credentials rotated to read-only, or a -config file naming a database nobody writes to any more all keep IsReplicating true until the restore. `o.Verification` (OFF by default) runs a real round trip on a schedule — upsert a sentinel row into `__rask_backup_probe` on the live DB (through Rask.SQLite's non-blocking busy-retry), wait `ReplicationGrace` (10s), `litestream restore` to a TEMP path (never beside the live DB; deleted on every path) and check the sentinel came back — publishing `status.Verification` (`Outcome`/`LastVerifiedAt`/`LastAttemptedAt`/`ReplicationLag`/`LastError`). Knobs: `Enabled=false`, `Interval=24h`, `VerifyOnStartup=false`, `ReplicationGrace=10s`, `PollInterval=15s`, `Timeout=2min`, `TempDirectory`, `BusyRetry`. THREE outcomes, not two: `Inconclusive` = the sentinel had not shipped yet (LAG, never page on it — alert on a `LastVerifiedAt` that stops moving), `Failed` = the restore failed or came back without the sentinel (THE alert), `Skipped` = no DatabasePath (config mode can manage several DBs, same choice RestoreAsync makes). EVERY PASS COSTS A RESTORE — a real download and real egress — which is why it is opt-in, daily by default, and must not be wired to a pollable health endpoint; `ISqliteBackupVerifier` is registered either way for on-demand passes. The verification restore passes `-o` (added in both URL and -config mode — config mode emitted none before, so it would have overwritten the live DB with a copy of itself) and DELIBERATELY OMITS `-if-replica-exists`, which would turn "no replica at all" into a silent pass. End-to-end proof against real MinIO in Docker: `scripts/verify-litestream-minio.sh`. Snapshot companion `Rask.SQLite.Snapshots` (docs/sqlite.md#scheduled-snapshots): scheduled CONSISTENT full-file backups via SQLite Online Backup API (`SqliteConnection.BackupDatabase`) — NO external binary, works on minimal/distroless + Alpine images. `services.AddRaskSqliteSnapshots(o => { DatabasePath; DestinationDirectory; Interval=6h; Retain=7; SnapshotOnStartup=false; BusyTimeout=30s; })` runs a hosted BackgroundService (PeriodicTimer) that snapshots + prunes to newest N; or inject `ISqliteSnapshotter` for on-demand `SnapshotAsync()`. Swap the `ISqliteSnapshotStore` (default DirectorySnapshotStore) for object storage; `store.ListAsync(ct)` reports what's held (name/size/timestamp, newest first, scoped to the store's search pattern) — a default interface impl returns empty, so a custom store must override it to be listable. Complements Litestream (streaming) or stands alone. Docker: mount a volume for DestinationDirectory or snapshots are lost on container removal; DB on local/named-volume not NFS/CIFS (WAL locking).
- [CQRS](docs/cqrs.md): the opt-in, standalone `Rask.Cqrs` package — a source-generated, reflection-free CQRS/mediator. IQuery<T>/ICommand/ICommand<T>/INotification + their handlers, dispatched via a single IDispatcher — QueryAsync for a query, SendAsync for a command (response type inferred either way) and PublishAsync for notifications; register with AddRaskCqrs(). Handlers are wired by a Roslyn generator (no runtime reflection, no assembly scanning, [DynamicDependency]-preserved ctors) so it publishes clean under the WASM/AOT trimmer. Pipeline behaviors (IPipelineBehavior<TRequest,TResult>, registered via AddOpenBehavior / AddBehavior) are the decorator hook for logging/validation/etc; none ship. Notifications fan out Sequential or WhenAll. Diagnostics RASK028 (ambiguous handler) / RASK029 (unregisterable handler). Depends only on Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection.Abstractions. **Remote dispatch** — the companion `Rask.Cqrs.Client` / `Rask.Cqrs.Server` packages let a WASM-hosted app reach its server through the SAME IDispatcher call it makes in-process: no HttpClient at the call site, no /api/* endpoints to write, and nothing on a message marks it remote (you write a record and a handler, and where the project sits decides where it runs). One line each — AddRaskCqrsClient() in the browser, AddRaskCqrsServer() + MapRaskCqrs() on the host — and neither half references the other, so a browser bundle cannot compile the endpoint code and the server never carries the browser transport; put the messages where both halves compile them — a Shared project, or one file Compile-linked into the host — and the handlers in the server only, which is what keeps a connection string or a pricing rule out of a download anybody can read. A client is a PURE client: every request message it dispatches travels, so a handler sitting in the client project is BYPASSED and the server answers 404 for a name it has no handler for — [LocalOnly] is the only way to keep a message in-process, and it is what a browser-local counter or offline queue needs; notifications are the deliberate exception, fanning out locally AND travelling, exactly once each. The wire is TWO endpoints, not one per message — GET and POST on /_rask/cqrs/request/{name}, the verb carrying what IQuery and ICommand already declare, so a command is 405 on GET and cannot be triggered by a URL, a prefetch or a link scanner (a query too long for a URL falls back to POST with an identical result); the literal route segments outrank the dashboard's /_rask catch-all and the SPA fallback, the name being a route segment gives logs/metrics/rate-limit partitions the message name for free, and MapRaskCqrs() returns the endpoint group for .RequireRateLimiting(...)/CORS/output caching. It fails closed: authenticated-by-default with [AllowAnonymous] the only way past, [Authorize] supplying a policy AND roles (both enforced), an anonymous caller getting the same answer for a real message name as for a typo so the endpoint cannot be walked to enumerate the app's messages, both verbs requiring the X-Rask-Cqrs header no cross-site markup can set, and handler exceptions becoming RFC 9457 problem+json with no exception text unless IncludeExceptionDetail is opted into. Failure to ARRIVE is the one thing remote dispatch adds — RemoteDispatchException, whose null StatusCode means the request never reached the server. [LocalOnly] on an INTERFACE covers a whole family, which matters because IBackgroundJob and IOutboxEvent both derive from ICommand — without it every job payload and outbox event would become an internet-reachable endpoint. Files go both directions with no adapter at the call site: a message declares a RaskFile directly and it uploads as multipart, a query returning FileDownload streams back with an attachment disposition, a safe-leaf filename and nosniff (navigator.Download(download) saves it); bounded by MaxUploadBytes/MaxFileCount, with chunked upload above ChunkedUploadThreshold, shipped in #764 — the server echoes X-Rask-Upload-Offset and answers 409 with its own offset on a mismatch, which the client reads and resumes from (#907, bounded per file). The two directions are NOT symmetric in the browser and the docs say which is which (#894): fetch has no request streaming, so a single-shot multipart upload costs its own size in the tab and ChunkedUploadThreshold is what bounds that — load-bearing, not a tuning knob; the download direction is streamed because the client asks for ResponseHeadersRead AND the WASM SDK defaults WasmEnableStreamingResponse to true, which the browser-rung publish gate now asserts on the shipped boot module because the default is the SDK's rather than Rask's. The two halves are put in front of EACH OTHER in tests/Rask.Cqrs.Transport.Tests — the only compilation that references both — and over a real browser fetch by the Rask.Example.Auth.WasmCookie journey (#896); note that AddRaskCqrsClient() installs its remote invokers into the PROCESS-WIDE CqrsRegistry the endpoint also dispatches through, so one process cannot host both halves. The wire codecs are source-generated Utf8JsonWriter/Utf8JsonReader code, not reflection, so remote dispatch publishes clean under the WASM/AOT trimmer; RASK053 reports a shape with no wire encoding and reaches no existing code, because codecs are generated only for a compilation referencing one of the two transport packages. `rask new --wasm` scaffolds the whole arrangement: the one-project build compiles one set of sources into both halves, so the messages need no Shared project, and the two csproj seams `RaskBrowserPackageReference` (a reference the bundle gets and the server does not) and `RaskBrowserStartup` (the type whose Configure(IServiceCollection) the bundle runs before the app) are what keep the two transports apart.
- [Browser APIs](docs/browser-apis.md): the map of all typed Web-API wrappers (53) — shared vs WASM-only, one-shot vs subscription, with the inject-from-ctor pattern and the push/[JSInvokable] mechanism. Every element component and every wrapper carries an XML `<summary>` that names its MDN reference page, and the generator forwards it (plus a `<param>` per documented property) onto the chain's entry and steps, so the documentation appears at the CALL SITE — hovering `Video` — not only on the type. BACKGROUND SYNC: `IBackgroundSync` (WASM only) wraps SyncManager + PeriodicSyncManager. The boundary is the whole design: the browser fires the sync even with the tab CLOSED, but the .NET runtime lives in the PAGE, not the service worker, so C# runs only while a client is open — Rask SW forwards the tag to every open client and the registration is otherwise consumed unseen. Hence: re-request tags at boot, keep the work in IIndexedDb/OPFS and let the sync be the NUDGE to drain it, and expect the win on a backgrounded tab rather than a closed one. Its SW handler deliberately stays out of rask-sw-shared.ts so the Server SW does not advertise a capability that cannot fire there. Periodic sync has no request API — check GetPeriodicPermissionAsync, do not ask. ANIMATION: `IWebAnimations` wraps Element.animate() — keyframes in the object form (Dictionary<string,string[]>, the shape the API takes natively and the one already in the source-gen JSON context), a handle back because an Animation cannot cross interop, an INVALID handle rather than a throw on a browser without the API, and WaitAsync returning false on cancel rather than rejecting. Reduced motion is the APP's call here, unlike view transitions, because only the app knows whether a given animation is an affordance or decoration. VIEW TRANSITIONS: `IViewTransitions` is the one wrapper an app could not have written itself — a same-document transition must WRAP the DOM mutation, and the mutation is the framework's morph, so enabling it routes the live runtime's own commit (diff and full-document, both hosts) through `document.startViewTransition`. Off by default, and off is byte-for-byte the previous timing; `prefers-reduced-motion` is honoured in the runtime because the animation is the browser's own default with no stylesheet of ours to switch off. REALTIME: `IWebRtc` (peer connections + data channels, every host), `IMediaStreams` (a MediaStream can't cross interop, so the framework holds it under a MediaStreamId and attaches it to a `<video>`), and `ISignaling` + the opt-in standalone `Rask.Signaling` package on the server (`AddRaskSignaling()` + `MapRaskSignaling()`, which needs `UseWebSockets()` or every upgrade 400s). The relay authenticates by default, mints peer ids server-side (never trusting the client's), delivers only within the sender's own room, and treats the payload as an opaque string end to end — it never parses an SDP or an ICE candidate.
- [JS interop](docs/js-interop.md): scoped CSS/TypeScript (a `.js` sibling is RASK055; tsgo compiles it, no npm), element refs, IJSRuntime, typed browser APIs — shared (both transports) in Rask.Core.Browser ( plus the PWA APIs IWebPush/INotifications/IBadge/IWakeLock, and the all-host headless Shareable — OS share sheet, attaches data-rask-share to your element and fires navigator.share in the click gesture so it works on Server too, plus the all-host GestureTrigger family — FullscreenTrigger/ScreenOrientationTrigger/EyeDropperTrigger/InstallTrigger/MediaCaptureTrigger/PictureInPictureTrigger, headless data-rask-gesture components that run activation-gated WASM-only APIs inside the click gesture so they reach the Server host declaratively); WASM-only in Rask.Wasm.Browser (IShare — code-driven share — plus IScreenOrientation/IFullscreen/IInstallPrompt + device APIs ISerial/IUsb/IHid/IBluetooth/IMediaDevices/IEyeDropper/IPictureInPicture/IIdleDetector).
- [AOT compilation](docs/aot.md): opt-in full WASM AOT via `-p:RaskWasmAot=true` (default keeps the Mono interpreter; needs the wasm-tools workload). A reflection-free `TypedParserRegistry` seeds every BCL `IParsable` primitive and resolves route/query/form string values with no runtime generics; the RoutesGenerator auto-registers custom `IParsable` route/query param types; `RaskBinding.RegisterParsable<T>()` registers custom form-model value types; `InvokeAsync<T>` needs a `JsonSerializerContext` for custom T. Runtime builds under `IsAotCompatible` and the WASM sample under `EnableAotAnalyzer`, so every warnings-as-errors build enforces AOT-safety; the full AOT publish runs nightly. Mono WASM AOT is mixed-mode (interpreter stays), so the win is a clean bundle + faster binding, not crash-avoidance.
- [Prerendering](docs/prerendering.md): a standalone WASM app has no server, so every visitor AND every crawler gets the boot shell — a spinner and the word "Loading" — because the real markup does not exist until megabytes of runtime have downloaded. `<RaskPrerender>true</RaskPrerender>` renders each route to real HTML at PUBLISH (build is untouched) and writes it beside the bundle as a DIRECTORY per route (`/about` → `about/index.html`), so a static host serves it at the URL the app routes to with no rewrite rule. Pages go through the same root boundary and the same wave loop a server's first response uses, each in its own DI scope — so a page whose `OnMountAsync` loads build-time data writes THE DATA, not its placeholder. A route is prerenderable when EVERY segment is a literal, decided on the parsed segments rather than by looking for a brace (the two agree today; only one keeps agreeing if the syntax grows a construct carrying no brace, or a literal containing one). **Skipped routes are reported by name, and reported even when the list is empty** — a parameterised route cannot be enumerated without the values and a catch-all is a 404 at best, so a pass that quietly covered a site's static half would read exactly like one that covered all of it. **A route that throws or does not settle is deliberately NOT written**: both still return perfectly ordinary HTML (an error document; the placeholder that was on screen when the budget ran out), and writing either publishes it under the route's own name with nothing saying so — a baked spinner is worse than no prerender because it LOOKS prerendered. The bundle still serves those routes at runtime, so it costs an optimisation rather than breaking the page; the usual cause is a page injecting a browser-only API. A pass that writes NO pages raises a build warning, asked of the OUTPUT rather than the exit code, because "it ran" and "it produced something" are different questions. HOW: a browser-wasm assembly cannot execute on the desktop, so the app's own sources compile a SECOND time for net10.0 into a companion in `obj/rask-prerender/` carrying the app's own project and package references — including `Program.cs`, deliberately, because that is where services are registered and `WasmHostBuilder.RunAsync` prerenders instead of booting when `RASK_PRERENDER_OUT` is set, so the app's REAL entry point drives the pass and there is no second place to keep registrations in sync. Engine is public for direct use: `RaskPrerender.PlanRoutes()` (`.Paths`/`.Skipped`) and `RaskPrerender.RenderDocumentAsync(app, services, budget)`, which takes no route on purpose — the caller holds the route table and seeds `RouteState.Path`. Check `Faulted`/`TimedOut` before writing. WASM only; per-page budget 30s.
- [Data layer](docs/data.md): the opt-in `Rask.Data` package — a provider-agnostic DDD base for EF Core apps. `Entity<TId>` (Id + CreatedAt/UpdatedAt audit stamps + a domain-events buffer via Raise/DomainEvents/ClearDomainEvents), opt-in marker interfaces ISoftDeletable (adds DeletedAt) / IVersioned (adds an int concurrency token), and three ISaveChangesInterceptors: AuditingInterceptor (stamps timestamps, bumps Version), SoftDeleteInterceptor (rewrites a Deleted ISoftDeletable to Modified + sets DeletedAt so db.Remove soft-deletes; global query filter DeletedAt==null hides it — use IgnoreQueryFilters() to see/restore), DomainEventInterceptor (after commit, publishes each entity's INotification events via Rask.Cqrs IDispatcher.PublishAsync in a fresh scope, then clears — but stands down automatically when something registers an IDomainEventDeliveryOwner, which AddRaskOutbox does, so an outbox app needs no option here; RaskDataOptions.DispatchDomainEventsInProcess (bool?, default null=auto) overrides in both directions). Wire with services.AddRaskData() (registers the interceptors + a TimeProvider) + o.AddInterceptors(sp.GetServices<ISaveChangesInterceptor>()) on the DbContext + modelBuilder.ApplyRaskConventions() in OnModelCreating (adds the query filter + IsConcurrencyToken). Optimistic concurrency: round-trip the original Version (hidden form field) and set Entry(x).Property(e=>e.Version).OriginalValue before SaveChanges → DbUpdateConcurrencyException on a stale save. BULK INSERT: `db.BulkInsertAsync(entities, o => o.BatchSize = 5000)` (also on DbSet<T>) fills the gap EF Core leaves — ExecuteUpdate/ExecuteDelete exist but bulk INSERT is explicitly out of EF's scope. Runs THROUGH the context so the interceptors still stamp/publish per row; batches the adds, turns AutoDetectChanges off, CLEARS the change tracker between batches (keeps a large load flat instead of quadratic — 100k rows: 942ms/1.16GB batched vs 1.25s/1.37GB for AddRange+SaveChanges vs 5.2s/2.59GB save-per-row). EACH BATCH COMMITS ON ITS OWN by default (SQLite has one write lock — a single transaction over a long import makes every other writer wait and the WAL hold every uncommitted page; the cost is that a failure leaves the committed batches). `o.SingleTransaction = true` makes the load all-or-nothing. THAT MODE, AND ANY AMBIENT TRANSACTION, REJECTS ENTITIES CARRYING DOMAIN EVENTS: DomainEventInterceptor publishes in SavedChanges, which inside a transaction runs BEFORE the commit, so a load failing at batch 7 would already have announced batches 1-6 — clear the events, drop the transaction, or use Rask.Outbox (same-transaction messages, drained after commit). FAST PATH `o.SkipChangeTracking = true`: writes the rows with ONE prepared single-row INSERT, parameters rebound per row, no entity entry ever materialised. OPT-IN because NO ISaveChangesInterceptor runs — not Rask's, not yours. The writer stamps CreatedAt/UpdatedAt itself from the SAME TimeProvider the AuditingInterceptor resolves (a frozen test clock agrees across both paths), but nothing stands in for the rest: entities carrying domain events are REJECTED, and an outbox never sees the load. Refuses-with-a-reason rather than writing wrong rows for: store-assigned integer keys, store-computed columns, shadow properties, navigations (nothing walks the graph), inheritance hierarchies, and a value-generated key left unset. A client-assigned Guid key (the Entity<Guid> shape) is fine — EF marks it ValueGenerated.OnAdd by convention, so the guard tests for STORE-supplied values, not OnAdd. DO NOT use a multi-row INSERT ... VALUES (..),(..) here: each distinct row count is a new statement to parse and Microsoft.Data.Sqlite binds by parameter NAME, so packing to the 32,766-parameter limit is quadratic (measured 192ms/7.2s/2.07min at 1k/10k/100k) and even a modest 200-row packing loses badly to prepared reuse. Throws if the context has pending changes (it clears the tracker, so it refuses rather than discard them); joins an ambient transaction instead of committing itself; under a retrying strategy a SingleTransaction load is one retryable unit with the sequence buffered for re-enumeration, while per-batch lets EF retry each batch with no replay. NON-OVERLAPPING RANGES: `modelBuilder.Entity<Booking>().HasNonOverlappingRange(x => x.StartsAt, x => x.EndsAt, partitionBy: x => x.RoomId)` declares that two rows may not cover the same point of a half-open [lo, hi) range — the booking/lease/price-period rule. SQLite has NO exclusion constraint and a UNIQUE index only stops IDENTICAL rows (100-200 and 150-250 both pass), so the rule is carried as provider-agnostic model metadata (a RangeExclusionSpec annotation naming PROPERTIES, resolved to columns by the provider so HasColumnName is honoured) and Rask.SQLite.EntityFrameworkCore's UseRaskSqlite emits an index + a BEFORE INSERT/BEFORE UPDATE trigger pair that RAISE(ABORT)s. HALF-OPEN is load-bearing: 100-200 and 200-300 are NEIGHBOURS, not a conflict; pair with a lo<hi check constraint since the rule assumes well-formed ranges. partitionBy scopes it (x => x.RoomId, or x => new { x.Sku, x.Region }); omit for table-wide. ignoreSoftDeleted defaults to TRUE for ISoftDeletable so a deleted row frees its slot, and is forced false otherwise (the column would not exist). A violating save throws RangeOverlapException naming the table, translated from SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_TRIGGER (1811) by an interceptor, instead of a raw code buried in DbUpdateException. Enforcement is IN THE DATABASE, so raw SQL/other processes are bound too — and a check-then-insert in app code would race. THE DDL IS RE-EMITTED AT THE END OF EVERY MIGRATION THAT TOUCHES THE TABLE, drop-then-create: SQLite cannot ALTER most things in place, so EF rebuilds the table (ef_temp_* -> copy -> DROP TABLE -> rename) and the DROP takes the triggers with it — attaching the DDL to CreateTable would silently retire the constraint on the next schema change. Arrives via migrations only: an existing table gains it from the next migration, EnsureCreated does not get it. Depends on Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore + Rask.Cqrs; server-side (not WASM). The base the soft-delete/concurrency/domain-event conventions build on.
- [Transactional outbox](docs/outbox.md): the opt-in `Rask.Outbox` package — durable, crash-safe domain-event delivery on the app's own EF Core database (no broker/Redis), the durable counterpart to Rask.Data's in-process publisher. Mark an event `IOutboxEvent` (: INotification); the `OutboxInterceptor` (SavingChanges) drains each tracked entity's IOutboxEvent domain events into `OutboxMessage` rows on the SAME context/transaction (atomic — never written for a rolled-back change), and the hosted `OutboxProcessor<TContext>` (BackgroundService, PeriodicTimer poll) publishes the oldest unprocessed batch via IDispatcher.PublishAsync and stamps ProcessedAt (or Attempts++/Error, retry to MaxAttempts) — at-least-once. Each message's outcome is saved on its OWN SaveChanges (not once per batch), so a row edited/deleted underneath the drain costs that one row instead of RE-PUBLISHING every event the batch already delivered; a failing poll is logged and retried rather than faulting the BackgroundService (which would stop the host). `OutboxOptions.RetentionPeriod` (default 7d, Zero=keep) purges PUBLISHED messages hourly in pages (delete-by-id, not one unbounded DELETE — the first sweep on a long-unpurged table would hold SQLite's write lock for its whole duration); dead letters have no ProcessedAt so retention can never match them. A source generator registers each IOutboxEvent type (name→Type) at module load so the drain deserializes with no runtime Type.GetType/scanning. Wire: `services.AddRaskCqrs()` + `services.AddRaskData()` (AddRaskOutbox claims delivery by registering an IDomainEventDeliveryOwner, resolved when the container is built, so the two calls work in either order and there is nothing to remember) + `services.AddRaskOutbox<AppDbContext>(o => { PollInterval=5s; BatchSize=100; MaxAttempts=10; })` + `.AddInterceptors(sp.GetServices<ISaveChangesInterceptor>())` on the context + `modelBuilder.AddRaskOutbox()` in OnModelCreating (maps OutboxMessage). Same INotificationHandler<T> reacts whether delivered in-process or via the outbox. Server-side; SQLite is single-writer so it polls, WAL+busy_timeout keep reads flowing; add an EF migration for the table. MULTI-INSTANCE IS SAFE: each processor LEASES the batch it claims — one UPDATE whose predicate re-tests claimability (portable, no SKIP LOCKED, no raw SQL), marking rows with a token + expiry (LeaseDuration, default 5m, must exceed PollInterval). A dead instance's lease simply expires and the work is claimable again — no sweeper. A lease stops one instance overwriting another's outcome; it does NOT make a side effect happen once (an instance overrunning its lease can have its row taken, and an email already sent is out) — at-least-once remains the contract. Attempts now counts attempts STARTED, not failures (the claim increments it), so a job that kills the process still reaches MaxAttempts; a first-time success shows Attempts=1. UPGRADING NEEDS A MIGRATION: `rask db add AddLeases && rask db update` — skip it and the processors throw every poll inside a catch, so the app looks healthy while doing nothing (they detect this case and log the two commands).  the tutorial's chapter 7 shows it.
- [Pillar metrics](docs/observability.md): each DB-backed pillar owns an OpenTelemetry-compatible `Meter` registered by its `AddRaskX` call — `Rask.Jobs`/`Rask.Outbox`/`Rask.Mail`, alongside the existing `Rask.Server`. Per pillar: `rask.<pillar>.processed|sent` + `.failed` (EVERY attempt, not every item) + `.deadlettered` (once, on the attempt that exhausts MaxAttempts) counters, a `.duration` histogram (ms), and `.pending`/`.deadletters` observable gauges. **`rask.*.deadletters` is the alert** — at-least-once with backoff means a pillar retrying itself to death still shows a healthy processed rate. Jobs/outbox tag by `job.type`/`message.type` (a closed set fixed at build time by the source generator); MAIL IS UNTAGGED ON PURPOSE (subject/recipient are unbounded → a time series per email). Queue-depth gauges are sampled on the processor's existing poll and ONLY while `metrics.WantsQueueDepth` (i.e. a listener subscribed) — never `COUNT(*)` inside the gauge callback, which a 1s collector would turn into continuous DB read load. `dotnet-counters monitor --counters Rask.Server,Rask.Jobs,Rask.Outbox,Rask.Mail`.
- [TypeScript front ends](docs/spa.md): a TypeScript SPA with a TYPED connection to your C#. **Rask supports TypeScript SPA clients only** — the framework is free — SEVEN templates (`react`, `preact`, `vue`, `angular`, `solid`, `svelte`, `lit`), exactly the set TanStack Query ships an adapter for, and every hosting rule is keyed on the BUNDLER's guarantee rather than on who generated it. **Angular keeps its own CLI**: its build IS Vite-based (@angular/build:application has run its dev server on Vite since v17) but create-vite has no angular template and the Vite config belongs to Angular, so `--template angular` runs `ng new` (kebab project name + --directory, because Angular rejects `Shop.Client`; --skip-install because the build installs, --skip-git because rask new inits one repo at the root) and THREE things differ — no vite.config.ts (the proxy is proxy.conf.json, pointed at from angular.json by a patch), `ng serve` on 4200 not 5173, and a bundle in dist/<project>/browser that the host is told about via a generated RaskSpaDistDir. `rask dev` reads the dev SCRIPT from the client's own package.json (`dev` for Vite, `start` for Angular) and the dev URL from the host's RaskSpaDevServerUrl, so neither is assumed, the language is not: a resolved client with no tsconfig.json fails the build with RASKSPA004, and `--template react` asks create-vite for `react-ts` rather than `react`. A refusal rather than a warning because a JS client CAN import the generated .ts (Vite transpiles it regardless) and gets none of what it is for — no inferred result type, no compile error on a renamed C# property, no refusal when a command is handed to raskQuery — so half the guarantee reads exactly like all of it until the wire disagrees. Two ways out: `RaskSpaTypeScriptConfig` names a config that isn't at tsconfig.json (a monorepo base config, a tsconfig.app.json), and `RaskEmitTypeScript=false` drops the contracts entirely, leaving UseRaskSpa a static-file host with no opinion about what produced the bundle. `rask new <name> --template react` runs the framework's OWN scaffolder (`npx create-vite@latest --template react-ts`) and overlays AT MOST FOUR files onto it — vite.config.ts (proxying /_rask to the host), the entry that installs the QueryClient, the component that dispatches, and (React and Solid only) src/router.tsx — plus two patches to create-vite's own output (the framework's TanStack packages into package.json, src/rask/ into .gitignore). **TanStack Router is scaffolded by default for react and solid**, the two adapters it ships, with routes declared IN CODE rather than through the file-based plugin (that plugin wants to own src/routes/, and this client is somebody else's scaffold); the others get no router rather than Rask picking one on the framework's behalf. Each entry point is the one its own scaffolder wrote — src/main.tsx for react/preact, src/index.tsx for solid, src/main.ts + App.vue for vue, App.svelte for svelte, src/my-element.ts for lit — because an overlay written for the wrong name does not fail, it lands beside the real file and is never imported. Svelte is the ONE template whose `build` script Rask rewrites (`svelte-check … && vite build`): create-vite gives it a bare `vite build` because tsc cannot read a .svelte file, so left alone a renamed C# property would break nothing at build time and surface on the wire. raskQuery/raskMutation import NOTHING from TanStack — every adapter exports its own `queryOptions`, so importing one would tie the bridge to one framework — and what differs per framework is only how the adapter wants them: `useQuery(raskQuery(m))` for react/preact, a THUNK for solid/svelte/lit and a `computed` for vue, which is what lets the options re-read the signal/rune/ref and refetch; everything else in the client is whatever Vite ships today, deliberately, because a hand-maintained React skeleton is a worse one within a release or two. Needs Node.js + a network at `rask new` time, which the C# templates do not, and the build ENFORCES a Node floor (`RaskSpaMinimumNode`, default 22.12.0) as **RASKSPA005** rather than letting vite fail with an engines error nobody reads — 22.12 because Vite's `^20.19.0 || >=22.12.0` is a range with a hole in it (21.x and 22.0-22.11 satisfy neither arm) and because Node 20 went EOL 2026-03-24. A floor is a minimum, not a recommendation: the scaffolded Dockerfile installs the current Active LTS (24), and Angular's CLI sets its own far higher floor and enforces it itself. Two projects, not three: a C#-on-both-halves solution needs a .Shared, but here the client's half of every contract is GENERATED TypeScript, so the messages live in the .Server. `--auth`/`--pwa`/`--push` are deliberately NOT accepted (they need client-side work — a React login flow, vite-plugin-pwa — this template does not write); `--cqrs` is not a flag because it is not optional (the wire IS the template); the DB batteries and `--docker` are. **The TypeScript is generated from the C# message records on every build** by a second backend over the same WireType model the wire codecs come from, so property names / enum encoding / null handling are decided ONCE: `await rask.dispatch(getOrder({ id }))` is an Order, inferred, with no wire name and no cast at the call site, and renaming a C# property breaks the front-end build instead of the wire. A source generator cannot write files, so the text rides out of the compiler as two string constants on an internal type and `Rask.Spa.Tasks` lifts them onto disk between CoreCompile and `npm run build` — read straight from the PE metadata (System.Reflection.Metadata), NOT by loading the assembly, which is what makes the WASM asset bake fragile under MSBuild node reuse (#650). Gated on `RaskEmitTypeScript` (set automatically when a client is resolved) because the whole front-end contract surface as a string literal is not something an in-process app should carry. **Dates**: DateTimeOffset/DateTime → a real JS `Date`, revived against a generated per-shape descriptor naming exactly the instant-bearing properties — NOT a JSON.parse regex reviver, which silently converts a product code or an ETag that merely looks like a timestamp; DateOnly/TimeOnly/TimeSpan/byte[] stay strings behind named aliases (DateOnly/TimeOnly/Duration/Base64), because `new Date("2026-08-25")` is UTC midnight and would render as the 24th anywhere west of UTC — the off-by-one the Gantt sample already documents. Prefer DateTimeOffset to DateTime on anything a front end reads: an Unspecified Kind writes an ISO string with no suffix, which modern JS parses as LOCAL time. Nothing is needed outbound — JSON.stringify already writes a Date as toISOString() (UTC, with a Z), which also means a round trip NORMALISES an Unspecified DateTime to UTC. The descriptor carries a container COUNT beside each nested shape, because Dictionary<string,T> and T both arrive as plain objects and without it the walk would revive a dictionary's own keys as the shape's properties. Display is Intl.DateTimeFormat's job, not Rask's. The client (client.ts + query.ts) is VENDORED into src/rask/ from the package and refreshed on every build, so upgrading Rask.Spa.Hosting upgrades both halves together; `raskQuery` accepts only a query (handing it a command is a compile error, mirroring the server's 405 on GET) and factories carry `.messageName`, so invalidation is never a string literal. **`rask dev`** starts TWO processes — `dotnet watch` for the host, `npm run dev` for the client — and points the browser at the BUNDLER (:5173), which proxies /_rask to :5000: HMR stays native and the browser sees one origin, so there is no CORS to configure. It passes `-p:RaskSpaBuild=false` (the dev server owns the client; a production bundle per save would make watch unusable) but the contracts are still emitted, because a dev server compiling the previous build's contracts is the exact failure the pipeline exists to prevent; the client process is killed with the host so a stale Vite cannot be picked up by the next session. **`app.UseRaskSpa()`** (standalone `Rask.Spa.Hosting`, referencing nothing else in Rask, so it fronts a plain ASP.NET app too) serves the bundler's dist/ — map your API FIRST, because UseRaskSpa ends the pipeline with a fallback to index.html and an endpoint mapped after it is shadowed rather than reached. A missing asset stays a 404 (the naive fallback answers a missing module import with HTML, which the browser reports as "Failed to load module script" — a broken framework rather than a missing file); cache classification is per bundler (Vite's index-DkK9xYz1.js, Angular's root-level hash) and NOT shared with the WASM host's dotnet.7a8b9c2d3e.js rule, because a wrong `immutable` sits in every visitor's cache for a year; index.html is never cached whatever the rules say; precompressed .br/.gz siblings keep the real content type; and in Development a missing build is answered 200 with the dev-server URL, not 503. `dotnet publish` copies the bundle into wwwroot, which the WASM host does not do and needs to — a baked absolute path names the build machine. `-p:RaskSpaBuild=false` skips node entirely and the app still compiles and still answers its API. The generated output is type-checked in the unit gate by tsgo (the native Go build of the TypeScript compiler, fetched as a checksum-verified BINARY at a PINNED version — that package publishes dated dev builds to `latest` — the same resolver the framework build uses, so the gate needs no npm and no Node and cannot be skipped for want of them), because a substring assertion cannot tell a well-formed type expression from a malformed one.
- [Blazor components](docs/blazor-components.md): a **real Blazor component** as an ordinary Rask component — from a Razor Class Library, MudBlazor, Radzen, any `ComponentBase`. Derive a `partial` class from `BlazorComponent<T>` and place it anywhere the chain goes. **The Razor SDK is neither replaced nor reconfigured**: it compiles `.razor` exactly as it always has, and Rask renders the result — which is why this costs nothing that can rot. **You do not redeclare parameters**: a Blazor component already states its surface, so the chain steps are read from its own `[Parameter]` properties, and `[BlazorParameter("Name")]` renames one whose name collides with a chain entry (`Title`, `Label`, `Form`, `Select` — CS0108, fatal under -warnaserror). **Server-rendered into the FIRST response**: the work runs from `OnPropsChangedAsync`, whose task lands in the page's quiescence scope, so a hosted component awaiting in `OnInitializedAsync` has finished before the HTML is sent rather than arriving a frame later — the whole value claim, and asserted on the real `QuiescentRender` wave path because `RaskTest.Render` is synchronous and could not prove it. **Parameters cross as live CLR objects** through `ParameterView`, not JSON: no wire vocabulary to violate, unlike a `.tsx` island's props. A nullable prop that is null OMITS its key — the OPPOSITE of the islands rule, because `ParameterView` is authoritative and writing null would CLOBBER the component's own default rather than mean "unset". **The hosted component's own `@onclick` fires with NO Blazor circuit**: Blazor assigns a real handler id to every event even in a static render and its own HTML writer simply drops them, so `BlazorFrameWriter` walks the render tree and writes Rask's `data-rask-on-*` instead — the click uses the delegated listener already in the page, travels the socket already open, and comes back through `DispatchEventAsync`. No SignalR, no `blazor.web.js`, no second connection; the same channel the React and Lit islands use. **An island is a LEAF in both families**: writing Rask children into a hosted component is a compile error (RASK062). No single crossing was right for all four `RenderFragment` shapes, and every wrong one failed silently or at render time. Compose the other way round — Rask chrome around the island. **A statically rendered island is deliberately NOT opaque**, and this is the trap: `FrameDiffer` SKIPS an opaque element's children, so an opaque static island would render new HTML on the server and never ship it — painting once and silently freezing. Opacity is reserved for a future circuit mode where the subtree really would belong to Blazor.
